scenes.heading: Normalization
scenes.narration: Normalization is the process of structuring tables to reduce redundancy and prevent inconsistent, duplicated data.

scenes.heading: Goals of normalization
bullets: Store each fact in exactly one place
Split data into related, focused tables
scenes.narration: Normalization eliminates duplicated data so the same fact is not repeated in many rows. It ensures each fact lives in exactly one place, which is the single source of truth. This prevents anomalies where an update or deletion leaves the data inconsistent. To achieve it, we split wide tables into smaller, focused tables connected by keys.

scenes.heading: Splitting a table to normalize it
scenes.narration: Before normalizing, a customer's name might be repeated in every one of their orders, wasting space and inviting inconsistency. After normalizing, the name lives once in the customers table, and orders simply reference it by customer_id. Now updating a customer's name means changing a single row. This is the core benefit of normalization: each fact is stored exactly once.

scenes.heading: Denormalized vs normalized
scenes.narration: A denormalized design repeats data and risks inconsistency, though it can be read with fewer joins. A normalized design stores each fact once and keeps data consistent, at the cost of more joins when querying. For transactional systems, that trade toward consistency is usually the right one.

scenes.text: Normalization removes redundancy so each fact lives in one place, keeping data consistent.
scenes.narration: The lasting lesson is that normalization removes redundancy by storing each fact once, which keeps transactional data consistent and easy to update.
